Like English, Spanish puts the article BEFORE the noun. The difference: Spanish articles change for masculine, feminine and plural.

One useful thing to notice: the masculine plural also means a mixed group.
“¿Tienes hermanos?” means “Do you have brothers OR sisters?”. The answer can be “Sí, tengo una hermana”.
As in English, the possessive goes BEFORE the noun and replaces the article: mi padre = my father (never “el mi padre”).
mi / tu / su do NOT change for gender: mi padre, mi madre. They only change in the plural: mis padres (unlike English, “my” gets an -s!). The exception is “nuestro / nuestra”.
“Su” can mean his, her, their or your (polite). The context makes it clear: “Pablo y su mujer” = Pablo and HIS wife.
“tu” without an accent = your; “tú” with an accent = you (pronoun). “Tu hermana” = your sister.
4. How to introduce someone: este / esta
When you point at a person or a photo, you use ESTE (this) for a man and ESTA (this) for a woman.
“esta” (this) has no accent; “está” (is, from ESTAR) has one. “Esta está aquí” = “This one is here”.
For “married / single” Spaniards usually use ESTAR: “Está casado”, “Estoy soltera”. You will also hear “Es soltero”, so both are accepted.
“Mayor” and “menor” compare age: “mi hermano mayor” = my older brother.
“La mujer” means “the woman”, but also “the wife”: “mi mujer” = my wife. For “husband” you say “el marido”.
